title: Why everyone's suddenly 'beauty maxxing': POLISHED
text:
Updated:  07:27 AEST, 21 September 2026

Welcome to Polished with Elise Wilson, where Daily Mail's qualified makeup artist and hair stylist answers your questions, shares advice, and trials the up-and-coming beauty and skincare trends so you don't have to.

I don't know what has happened to my algorithm lately, but I'm inundated with ridiculously stunning, confident, mostly-single women in their glow-up era.

While epic before and after transformations like these are absolutely nothing new, especially on Instagram, there's now a name for the increasingly strategic pursuit of becoming the most polished version of yourself.

Let me introduce you to the latest self-improvement obsession sweeping the beauty world: 'beauty maxxing'.

Before you confuse it with 'looksmaxxing', the controversial internet movement that first gained traction in the Andrew Tate corner of the web with its focus on maximising physical attractiveness, the two are most definitely not the same thing.

Beauty maxxing focuses on upgrading everything in your life from skincare, haircare and makeup to personal style, fitness, sleep and general wellbeing.

Yes, it can extend to cosmetic treatments and injectables for those who want them, but at its core the idea more broadly promotes working out what makes you look and feel your best, then being strategic about enhancing it.

And no one on my feed appears to be embracing it quite as enthusiastically as Dr Ewoma Ukeleghe, or simply Dr Ewoma as she's known to her 398,000 Instagram followers.

Beauty columnist Elise Wilson (pictured) says her feed is suddenly inundated with stunning women in their glow-up era. Now, the strategic pursuit of becoming the most polished version of yourself has a name - 'Beauty Maxxing'

The award-winning UK medical and cosmetic doctor has blown up online over the past year thanks to her refreshingly no-BS commentary on everything from skincare and aesthetic treatments to products and dating – although I think the latter deserves an entirely separate column, because that woman has some strong opinions.

But it's arguably the documentation of her own transformation that has gripped her followers the most.

Dr Ewoma regularly shares before and after photographs showing how much her appearance has evolved over the years and, refreshingly, she isn't pretending it happened because she started adopting J.Lo's 'anti-ageing secret' of slathering herself in olive oil.

She openly discusses everything from skincare, wigs and makeup to cosmetic dentistry, laser skin treatments and injectables, while her signature glass-like skin and impossibly smooth, shimmering décolletage have practically become characters in their own right.

In one recent video, Dr Ewoma explained that the goal should be to become 'the most beautiful version of yourself', rather than attempting to replicate another woman you've seen on Instagram.

She's also clear this isn't supposed to be one of those ridiculous seven-day glow-up challenges. Instead, her advice is aimed at women prepared to 'invest the time, the energy, and the coin' into gradually elevating their appearance.

And 'coin' is certainly the operative word here.

Once you start looking at everything that can fall under the beauty-maxxing umbrella, the calculations can start adding up pretty quickly, but experts say you can cherry-pick the most important ones before you completely break the bank.

Beauty maxxing is about upgrading every aspect of your routine, from skincare, hair and makeup to personal style, fitness and wellbeing, with cosmetic treatments and injectables also in the mix for those who want them. (Pictured: Online beauty sensation Dr Ewoma Ukeleghe)

Leading the beauty maxxing charge is UK medical and cosmetic doctor Dr Ewoma Ukeleghe, whose dramatic transformation has captivated her followers. She openly credits everything from skincare, wigs and makeup to cosmetic dentistry, lasers and injectables for her glow-up, and has quickly become the poster girl for this growing social media beauty phenomenon

So what does beauty maxxing actually involve?

The appeal is that there isn't one prescribed formula, nor does it necessarily require an enormous budget.

For some women, it might mean finding a haircut that suits their face, learning which colours flatter their complexion, improving their skincare routine, or working out which makeup enhances their features and ditching the rest.

There's even a distinction between 'soft maxxing' and 'hard maxxing'. Soft maxxing covers more accessible, non-invasive changes including skincare, makeup, haircare, teeth whitening, styling, sleep and hydration, while hard maxxing moves into cosmetic procedures, orthodontics, injectables and plastic surgery.

On paper, I actually quite like the idea.

I've worked in beauty for close to two decades, so I'm hardly going to sit here and tell you there's anything wrong with wanting to look your best.

I love treatments, makeup and a good laser, and I've spent a significant (maybe unhinged) amount of my career investigating the extremes of it all.

But this is also where beauty maxxing starts to make me slightly uncomfortable, because when the entire premise is about constantly becoming a better-looking version of yourself, where exactly are we supposed to stop?

There's even a distinction between 'soft maxxing' and 'hard maxxing'. Soft maxxing covers more accessible, non-invasive changes including skincare, makeup, haircare, teeth whitening, styling, sleep and hydration, while hard maxxing moves into cosmetic procedures, orthodontics, injectables and plastic surgery

When does 'your best self' become never good enough?

One piece of advice from Dr Ewoma particularly stuck with me.

When discussing injectables, she recommended establishing what she calls a 'ceiling of happiness' before you begin - essentially deciding what you're trying to improve and at what point you're going to be satisfied.

Without that end point, she warns, 'it's very easy to get carried away'.

I've previously written about looking back at old photographs and realising I had more filler through my cheeks and jawline than I thought I did at the time.

And that's the thing about continually tweaking your appearance - your baseline starts to move very quickly.

Dr Ewoma has previously described Botox as a 'gateway drug' on the Hot Smart Rich podcast, joking that it rarely stops there, and while the wording is provocative, I understand exactly what she means.

Social media has effectively turned our faces and bodies into never-ending renovation projects, with another treatment, device or perceived flaw waiting around every corner.

Dr Ewoma recommends setting a 'ceiling of happiness' before having injectables, deciding what you want to improve and when enough is enough, warning it can otherwise be 'very easy to get carried away'. (Pictured on the Hot Smart Rich podcast with host Maggie Sellers Reum)

Start with the basics

Perhaps the most refreshing part of Dr Ewoma's approach is that she doesn't immediately send women running towards a clinic.

She starts with the decidedly unsexy basics of grooming, including moisturising your body, looking after your oral health, finding a fragrance you love and keeping your nails groomed.

From there, she recommends learning which colours suit you. After having an in-depth colour analysis in Korea, Dr Ewoma discovered she was a 'deep autumn' and even learned that the stark white clothing she loved wasn't actually her most flattering shade.

As a 'warm, pure autumn' myself, I can absolutely relate, and I'd urge everyone to have their colours professionally analysed at least once in their lifetime.

When it comes to makeup, rather than buying another viral foundation because it looked incredible on someone on TikTok, she recommends learning how to apply makeup to your features and even suggests booking a one-on-one lesson with a makeup artist.

Seriously, knowing where your blush should sit, which foundation works with your skin and how to enhance your eye shape will do far more for you than owning 14 half-used palettes.

Another hack: learning which colours best suit your complexion and how to apply makeup to enhance your individual features. A professional colour analysis and one-on-one makeup lesson are worthwhile beauty investments according to the experts

Don't overdo the 'hair maxxing'

Beauty maxxing has inevitably made its way north to our scalps too, with 'hair maxxing' videos now packed with rosemary oil, scalp massage, microneedling, supplements and laser devices promising thicker, healthier locks.

But trichologist and AGWÉ Haircare founder Adrian De Brock warned that more certainly doesn't mean better.

While he believes the trend can be positive when it encourages people to take a proactive approach to their wellbeing, problems arise when optimisation turns into over-treatment.

Hair follicles respond slowly, he explained, and aggressively stimulating the scalp or piling on products can disrupt the scalp barrier, cause inflammation and increase breakage.

For pattern hair loss, Adrian pointed to topical minoxidil as having substantially more clinical evidence behind it than viral oils and gummies, while microneedling has encouraging evidence in certain circumstances but should be approached carefully.

He also warned that burning, itching, redness, tenderness, excessive flaking or pustules aren't signs that a product is 'working'.

'Your scalp is a delicate ecosystem and can easily be thrown off balance and become reactive,' he said, recommending people slowly introduce treatments rather than trying everything at once.

At-home technology has also become a huge part of the trend, particularly LED masks and red-light devices. Victoria Hiscock, STYLPRO's Beauty Technology Spokesperson says consumers should look beyond attention-grabbing claims about the number of LEDs in a device, with factors such as wavelength, irradiance and dose also important

What about the skin?

This is where beauty maxxing gets particularly tempting for me because, as anyone who regularly reads this column will know, I will try almost anything in the pursuit of great skin.

Dr Ewoma considers skin the foundation of the entire process but recommends beginning with the basics like a good cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen.

From there, additional products should be chosen according to your actual skin type, concerns and goals rather than whatever bottle is currently going viral.

For those wanting to take things further, there are prescription topicals and professional treatments ranging from facials and microneedling to lasers and energy-based devices, although Dr Ewoma warns that stronger skincare can cause problems when used incorrectly and recommends seeking specialist advice.

At-home technology has also become a huge part of the trend, particularly LED masks and red-light devices.

Victoria Hiscock, STYLPRO's Beauty Technology Spokesperson, believes beauty maxxing can be positive when it encourages consistency, but warns 'it's easy to fall into the trap of thinking maximum optimisation is the goal', which could reinforce unrealistic expectations of perfection.

When it comes to red-light therapy, she said consumers should look beyond attention-grabbing claims about the number of LEDs in a device, with factors such as wavelength, irradiance and dose also important.

One area that's easy to overlook while we're obsessing over skin and hair is our teeth, yet a brighter, healthier-looking smile can make an enormous difference to someone's overall appearance

Don't forget your smile

One area that's easy to overlook while we're obsessing over skin and hair is our teeth, yet a brighter, healthier-looking smile can make an enormous difference to someone's overall appearance.

According to Georgina Northcott, the founder of Sydney clinic Teeth Whitening Boutique, coffee, tea, red wine, smoking, strongly coloured foods and plaque or tartar build-up can all dull teeth, while ageing naturally allows more yellow-toned dentine to show through as enamel becomes thinner.

Her advice is to start with regular dental checks and cleans, brushing twice daily and flossing before considering cosmetic whitening.

The clinic's signature 80-minute Boutique Session costs $399, which gives you some indication of how quickly even 'soft' beauty maxxing can start adding up, but results do last well.

Dr Ewoma has also spoken openly about having composite bonding on several teeth, which she credits with transforming her smile, although she strongly recommends discussing your options with a qualified dentist rather than chasing the whitest or most dramatic result possible.

Elise recently had her teeth gleamed at Sydney clinic Teeth Whitening Boutique. The clinic's signature 80-minute Boutique Session costs $399, which gives you some indication of how quickly even 'soft' beauty maxxing can start adding up, but results do last

The syringe at the end of the rainbow

Dr Ewoma is remarkably open about having injectables herself and says they transformed her face, but she is equally adamant they should be performed conservatively.

Her overarching philosophy is that less is more, and one of her most interesting pieces of advice is to stop bringing injectors photographs of other women - or AI-generated versions of ourselves - as inspiration.

Instead, she suggests bringing an old photograph of yourself as the reference point for a more realistic outlook of what can be achieved.
